    async def async_clear_usercode(self, code_slot: int) -> bool:
        """
        Clear a usercode on a code slot via the User->Credential primitives.

        Slot-only providers address the credential by slot and delete it
        directly. Native-user providers must target the credential's actual
        owning user, which is not assumed to equal the slot index: a
        credential may have been created on the lock by another controller,
        or the integration may have allocated a user identifier that differs
        from the slot. The owning ``user_id`` is resolved from the lock's
        current users and threaded through the ``CredentialRef`` so the
        provider's delete primitive can address the credential precisely.
        The lock-side user stays put; it is torn down only when the slot
        is removed from LCM config (see ``async_release_managed_slot``).
        Returns True if the value changed, False if it was already cleared
        -- and True when the provider cannot determine whether a change
        occurred. Either way the worker reads the slot back.

        A clear adopts no untagged user (#1518). Adoption belongs to the set
        path, where the write that follows tags the user and corrects a wrong
        guess; a clear is an end state -- a slot turned off or released --
        and nothing follows it to correct anything. The untagged user holding
        a PIN at that index is as likely to be one the homeowner made in the
        vendor's app as ours. The cost: a pre-tag install's PIN in a slot

content.text:
Here's what I found about the device index, which you decided on 2026-09-16 ("each credential type gets its own index on the lock, chosen when first set").

- On native-user locks (Z-Wave User Credential CC, Matter), LCM **finds its credentials through the tagged lock user** (`lcm:<slot>:`), not through the index (`_base.py:1273-1330`). The lock user is a persistent anchor: clearing a PIN leaves the user in place, and releasing a slot removes the user only "when it holds nothing else" (`_base.py:1768`).
- That makes your per-type index cheap for password. The Z-Wave provider can look up the tagged user's password credential wherever it sits. If there isn't one, it takes the lowest free password index. Matter already lets the lock pick the index (`credential_index_follows_slot = False`), so this follows an existing pattern. **Nothing needs to persist the index, and the sync core never sees it.** The address stays `(slot, password)`.
- PIN keeps following the slot on Z-Wave (`credential_index_follows_slot`), which your 09-16 note already leaned toward for back-compat.
- Release has to change in one place. Today it removes "its PIN, and the user itself only when it holds nothing else". It now has to remove the password LCM wrote as well. Otherwise a deleted user's password still opens the door, which is the #1453 bug again for a second type.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The user tag is what makes indexes free to move. Because LCM identifies its user by the tag and not by position, any credential type can sit at any index on that user. The tag rule from #1422 ("mutable values never go in identifiers") is what makes per-type indexes nearly free here.
- Virtual has no user records and keys by slot, so on Virtual the password index simply equals the slot. Only Z-Wave User Credential CC needs the allocation.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

I have what I need for the first section. I'll present the design in parts and check each with you before moving on.

## Design, part 1 of 4: sync core and storage

**Credential address.** `CredentialAddress(slot, type)` already exists in `model/credentials.py`. It becomes the key throughout `sync/`:
- `LockWorker.slots: dict[CredentialAddress, Slot]`. `want`, `forget`, `status` and `push` take an address.
- `LockPort.read(addresses) -> {address: Reading}` and `LockPort.write(address, value)`.
- `sync/slot.py` keeps its single-value state machine. Only the names change: `Holds.pin` becomes `Holds.value` and `Want` becomes `str | None` for any type. `Holds.__repr__` keeps masking the value.
- Release stays per slot. When a slot leaves the entry, the worker releases every type it holds there in one provider call, so the provider can delete the lock user only after its last credential is gone.

**Which addresses a lock manages.** The managed addresses for a lock are the user's slot crossed with the intersection of `capabilities.credential_types` and `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, computed **per lock**. A lock without password never gets a password address, so it can't make the aggregate `in_sync` unavailable. This fixes the global `managed_addresses()` gap found in the #1572 review. `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` becomes `{PIN, PASSWORD}`. The available types for an entry are the union over its locks, and that union drives which entities and card tabs exist.

**Persistence (`ha/lock_store.py`, Store v1 → v2).** Each slot record becomes `{"wrote": {"pin": <fingerprint>, "password": <fingerprint>}, "release": …}`. The migration moves an existing `wrote` under `"pin"`. The fingerprint also takes the type as input (`fingerprint(type, value, salt)`), so a PIN and a password with the same text don't produce the same fingerprint. No credential value is ever persisted, same as today.

**Config.** The user subentry gets an optional `password` alongside `pin`. Because it's optional and absent means "none", no config-entry migration is needed. The enable rule becomes "at least one credential of a type the entry offers". `pin_required` becomes `credential_required`, with a repair to match.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Keeping release at slot level while sync goes per address mirrors the lock itself. A lock user owns all of its credentials, and deleting the user deletes them all. If release went per address, the provider would have to work out when it was handling the last credential on the user.
- The Store migration is the only one-way step in this design. Everything else is additive, so if it ships as a minor release, a downgrade only fails to read v2 Store records. Downgrading is the case HA's `Store` versioning exists to refuse.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

| `ha/slot_coordinator.py:355`, enable toggle | Enabling without a PIN raises `PinRequiredError` and the `pin_required` repair | Refused only when the user has no credential of any type. Becomes `CredentialRequiredError` and the `credential_required` repair |
| `config_flow.py:84-93, 422`, setup and subentry forms | `_slot_enabled_without_pin` | `_slot_enabled_without_credential`, which checks every managed type's field |
| `switch.py:62`, `ha/services.py:451`, `repairs.py:179`, `__init__.py:1220` | Catch, route or clean up `pin_required_*` | Same for `credential_required_*`. Startup deletes any leftover `pin_required_*` issue so it doesn't linger after the upgrade |

There's one edge case I'll decide unless you object: a user whose only credential is a password, in an entry whose last password-capable lock was removed. Under the "keep the value, hide the entity" decision the password is still stored, so by your rule the user stays enabled. Each lock then correctly holds nothing for them, and their `in_sync` is on. I'll count any stored value, as you said, rather than "a value some lock can take".

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Counting stored values instead of currently-writable values keeps the enable state a pure function of the config. If it depended on lock capabilities, a lock dropping offline or getting re-interviewed could flip users between enabled and disabled. That's the coupling the condition → `allowed` gate work moved away from.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Design, part 2 of 4: providers

**Z-Wave (`providers/zwave_js.py`)**
- **Capabilities.** `async_get_capabilities` also reports `PASSWORD` from the same `supported_credential_types` read it already uses for PIN: slot count, min/max length, and `supports_learn`. A lock that doesn't advertise password is unchanged.
- **Read.** User records already carry password credentials. The PASSWORD type is already mapped (`zwave_js.py:163`). A read for `(slot, password)` finds the user tagged `lcm:<slot>:` and returns that user's password credential, wherever it sits, as `Holds`, `MASKED`, or `EMPTY`.
- **Write.** Look up the tagged user's password credential and overwrite it in place. If there isn't one, take the **lowest password index no user holds**, taken from the user list read just before the write. The user record is created on the first write of either type, the same way PIN works today.
- **Clear.** Delete only that password credential. The user stays as the anchor.
- **Release.** Remove every credential LCM wrote to the user (PIN and password), then remove the user only if it holds nothing else. A card or credential added in the vendor's app still protects the user from deletion.

**Virtual.** It already advertises every type. Its password is keyed by slot, like its PIN.

**Everything else** (Matter, ZHA, Z2M, Schlage, Akuvox, zwave-js-ui MQTT): no change. They don't advertise password, so the per-lock address rule from part 1 never gives them a password address.

**Base (`providers/_base.py`)**
- `_assert_slot_within_capacity` keeps checking the PIN count only, since password doesn't follow the slot.
- A password write on a lock with no free password index raises `LockOperationUnsupported`, naming the lock and its password slot count. The slot then holds with `CANT_SET`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- "Lowest index no user holds" has to come from the lock's user list, not from LCM's own records. A vendor-app credential at index 1 is invisible to LCM's store but very visible to the lock, and overwriting it would silently replace a code someone else added. This is the same "allocation refuses to write over a code it can still read" rule that `_base.py:1783` states for slots.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Does part 2 look right? One thing to check: when a lock is out of password indexes, I've made that a per-slot `CANT_SET` hold, the same as a PIN slot past capacity, not an entry-level error.

I'm thinking through how `lock_codes` represents the worker's view of a lock, keyed by address, and noting that for passwords the LCM slot number differs from the device index—so a managed password appears under the user's slot rather than its underlying device position.

Now I'm weighing three options for the lock card: adding type tabs for PIN vs. password, grouping both credential types under each slot chip, or leaving the lock card PIN-only for now and pushing password visibility to the slot card as a follow-up.

I lean toward tabs for consistency with the slot card, since PIN and password each have their own capacity on the lock, though empty-range grouping would need a password index space we don't currently model.

For now the provider only reads credentials tied to tagged users, so showing unmanaged passwords would require a fuller credential listing — out of scope for a first release, so I'd just show managed entries plus a count.

I'll present this as an open question with a text comparison of options rather than a full mockup, recommending tabs on the lock card when supported, matching the slot card pattern.

The PIN tab stays as-is; the password tab shows one chip per managed user holding a password on that lock, labeled by slot and name with sync state and a masked reveal, though I'd skip a true capacity count since that needs unmanaged credentials too — flagging that as a follow-up. I'll identify chips by user name and slot number rather than raw device index, then pose this as a question to the user.

content.text:
The lock card is a different question from the slot card. The slot card shows one user. The lock card (`ts/lock-codes-card.ts`) shows **what one lock holds**: one chip per position on the lock, with ranges of empty positions collapsed ("Slots 4–10"), managed codes linked to their entry, and unmanaged codes editable through `write_unmanaged_code`. Its data is the worker's view of the lock (`websocket.py:644`, `lock_codes()`), keyed by slot.

Password breaks the card's main assumption, that a chip's number is a position on the lock:
- On Z-Wave, a PIN's lock index **is** the slot, so the PIN chips stay accurate.
- A password sits at an index LCM chose. The worker knows it as `(slot 20, password)`, and the index exists only inside the provider.
- In the first release, a password LCM doesn't manage (one added in the vendor's app) has no address at all, so the worker never sees it.

Three ways to handle it:

1. **Type tabs on the lock card** (recommended). The tabs match the slot card and appear only when the lock takes more than one managed type. The **PIN tab is exactly today's card.** The **Password tab** has one chip per user holding a password on this lock, labeled with the user's name and slot, the entry, sync state, and the masked value with reveal. It has no empty-position ranges, because LCM doesn't model password positions, and no unmanaged editing. Each type has its own capacity and length limits on the lock, so splitting by type matches how the lock itself is organized.
2. **Both credentials on each managed chip.** A managed user's chip gains a password line under the PIN. There are no tabs, but the chip's number now means "user" for one line and "position on the lock" for the other. A user who has only a password needs a chip with no PIN position, which the ranges and grouping logic (`_renderGroupsWithBorrowing`) wasn't built for.
3. **The lock card stays PIN-only for now.** Passwords appear only on the slot card, with a follow-up issue for the lock card. This is the least work, but a lock holding LCM passwords looks like it holds less than it does, which is exactly what this card exists to show.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Option 2's trouble comes from one integer meaning two things: the lock's index for a PIN, and LCM's slot for a password. Mixing those up is the "mutable values in identifiers" problem from #1422 again. Tabs avoid it because each tab has its own number space.
- Showing unmanaged passwords later doesn't need a new read. A Z-Wave User Credential read already returns every user with all of their credentials, vendor-app ones included. The Password tab can grow an "unmanaged" section later without the sync core knowing about it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Now I'm thinking through Part 3 on entities and validation, planning to split the current text-entity handling into separate `PinText` and `PasswordText` subclasses under a shared `CredentialText` base, each carrying its own credential type and pattern, then moving into Part 4 covering config, services, websocket, and card plus testing.

I need to decide on validation: PIN should stay unchanged without a pattern since existing stored PINs may include non-digit characters, but Password should get a printable-ASCII pattern enforced through a single shared `validate_credential_value` function used consistently across the entity, config flow, services, and coordinator. The open question is whether to strip whitespace from passwords like PIN does, since stripping could unintentionally alter a passphrase that legitimately contains spaces.

I'm deciding not to strip passwords since spaces are valid characters, even though that risks accidental trailing spaces from masked input fields. For length validation, I need the coordinator to check only against password-capable locks rather than all locks, and the entity setup should create per-type entities dynamically while preserving stored values when a type becomes unavailable. I also need to extend pin-masking to cover any credential type generically, ensure diagnostics redact password fields the same way pins are redacted, and handle duplicate credential refusal and per-type in-sync sensors consistently.

I want to generalize the pin generator to also produce passwords respecting each lock's length constraints, confirm that the credential_used event automatically includes passwords once added to the MANAGED set, and check how existing in_sync sensor keys are named on main before extending that pattern to passwords.

content.thinking: The in-sync sensor class setup looks right, disabled by default except for the aggregate. I should add "password": "Password" to CREDENTIAL_LABELS so it flows into sensitive key redaction and the in-sync naming automatically, matching the TS contract test. Now moving on to Part 3.

content.text:
Most of the per-type machinery already exists on `main`. Part 3 mostly connects password to it.

## Design, part 3 of 4: entities and validation

**Text entities (`text.py`)**
- Split `LockCodeManagerText` into `LockCodeManagerNameText` and a `LockCodeManagerCredentialText` base. The base holds `credential_type`, `TextMode.PASSWORD`, and a class-level `_attr_pattern`. `PinText` and `PasswordText` subclass it. `async_set_value` loses its `if self.key == CONF_PIN` branch and becomes `coordinator.async_request_credential_update(self.credential_type, value)`.
- **`PasswordText.pattern = r"^[\x20-\x7E]*$"`.** The `*` lets `""` through, so clearing still works.
- **`PinText` gets no pattern in this work.** HA re-checks `pattern` when it renders the state (`text/__init__.py:174`), so a stored PIN with a non-digit character would make the entity fail to render after the upgrade. A PIN pattern would need its own audit and migration, so it stays out of scope here.
- `native_min` and `native_max` stay permissive for both types, for the three reasons in `text.py:73-104`.
- Entities exist for **the types the entry offers** (the union across its locks). When a type stops being offered, its entity is removed and the stored value is kept (your 09-16 decision).

**One validator, every entry point.** A new `model/credentials.py` function, `validate_credential_value(type, value)`, checks the character set: digits for PIN, printable ASCII for password. The text entity's pattern, the config flow, `add_user` / `set_credential`, and the coordinator all call it, so YAML and services can't store a value the entity would then fail to render. **Passwords aren't stripped**, because a space is a legal character in one. PINs keep `vol.Strip`.

**Length, per lock.** `_validate_credential_length(value, type)` is already generic (`slot_coordinator.py:303`). It just gets called with `PASSWORD`, checking only the locks that take password. The error already names each lock and its range: "PASSWORD length 5 is not accepted by all locks: 8-32 characters for Front Door".

**Already per-type, so this is one line.** Add `"password": "Password"` to `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` (`const.py:210`, mirrored in `ts/const.ts`, which a contract test checks). That one line gives you:
- a `password_in_sync` sensor that's disabled by default (`binary_sensor.py:163`) while the aggregate `in_sync` stays enabled;
- password added to `SENSITIVE_ENTITY_KEYS`, so diagnostics redact it;
- `credential_used` events listing password once it's a managed type (`event.py:122`).

**Other rules**
- **Duplicates.** Setting a password another user in the entry already has is refused. The same text as someone's PIN is allowed.
- **Masking.** `Holds.__repr__` already masks the value. `mask_pin` becomes `mask_credential` and is used in every log line that carries a credential value.
- **Generator.** `generate_pin` becomes `generate_credential(type, length)`. For password it draws from the same printable-ASCII set and lands inside the length range of every password-capable lock in the entry.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The three uses of `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` are why the #1572 per-type sensor work paid off. The labels map was built as a single switch for "which types exist", and password is the first time it gets used for that.
- A pattern only constrains values going forward, but HA checks it when rendering values that are already stored. That's why the validator has to cover every way a value can get in (YAML, services, flows), not only the entity.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Does part 3 look right? Two choices to check: no pattern on PIN for now, and passwords not stripped.

content.thinking:
I'm realizing that skipping pattern validation here actually matters for security — the pattern-mismatch error message exposes the raw value in cleartext, so for a password field that would leak the password directly in the exception text.

Since text.set_value also routes through async_set_value into the coordinator's own validator, the pattern constraint is redundant anyway. I'll recommend dropping the pattern attribute and double-check that the coordinator's own ServiceValidationError messages never include the raw value, including the length-check error.

Now moving to part 4, covering config flow changes for password fields, service and websocket payload updates to support credential types beyond PIN, and how the card consumes this new structure.

On the UI side, I'm thinking through tabbed interfaces for slot, add-user, and lock cards with per-type sync indicators and input modes, plus flagging blueprints that might assume PIN-only data. For testing, I'm laying out the order from property-based tests through e2e with Virtual and Z-Wave providers down to unit tests.

I need a sourced Z-Wave node dump showing password credential capability rather than inventing test data, plus a mutation check on per-lock address filtering when password release occurs. I'm phasing the PR into four reviewable stages: a no-behavior-change re-key to CredentialAddress with Store v2 migration first, then the model/validation layer adding PASSWORD support end-to-end with Virtual, then the Z-Wave provider capabilities, and finally the UI cards.

Since PR2 enabling PASSWORD before cards exist would expose entities without UI, I'll keep all four PRs merged before cutting the release — a minor additive release with the Store migration, no user-facing back-compat concerns since it's all internal websocket. I want to keep that last card PR reasonably concise.

content.text:
Agreed. Drop it. The deciding reason is something I didn't mention before: **HA's pattern error puts the value itself in the message.**

```python
# homeassistant/components/text/__init__.py:82-86
raise ValueError(
    f"Value {value} for {entity.entity_id}"
    f" doesn't match pattern {entity.pattern}"
)
```

A password with a tab or an emoji in it would show up in cleartext in the frontend toast and in any log that records the exception. The `native_min`/`native_max` checks have the same leak (lines 73-80), which is one more reason the PIN entity already avoids them.

Dropping it costs nothing. `text.set_value` ends in `entity.async_set_value`, which calls the coordinator, so `validate_credential_value` still checks every value. It also gives a better error: "Password may only contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces", with no value echoed and no regex shown. It also removes the render-time failure, so the PIN and password entities end up following the same rule.

Updated part 3: **neither credential entity sets `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. The validator and the per-lock length check in the coordinator are the only gates, and their errors never include the value.**

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- This is the third time HA's built-in `TextEntity` validation has been the wrong tool here: min blocks clearing, max cuts off typing silently, and pattern leaks the value. Each was reasonable on its own. Together they amount to a rule: in this integration, credential entities are thin pipes, and all validation lives in the coordinator.
- Holding to "errors never include the value" needs a test. A coordinator test can submit a value with a known marker (an invalid character plus a unique string) and assert the marker appears in neither the raised message nor `caplog`.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Design, part 4 of 4: config, services, cards, testing, PR order

**Config and services**
- The user subentry form gets an optional `password` field, shown only when one of the entry's locks takes password. Setup YAML gets `password:` per user.
- `add_user` gets `password`. `set_credential` and `clear_credential` already take `credential_type`. The `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` gate in `ha/services.py:186` opens on its own once password is in the set.
- Before release, check the blueprints and `services.yaml` for PIN-only assumptions. A shipped blueprint isn't type-checked, so this is a manual check.

**Websocket.** The card ships with the integration, so these payloads are internal and can change freely.
- `subscribe_code_slot` gains `credentials: {pin: {...}, password: {...}}`, each with value-or-length, `in_sync` and state, plus `available_types`.
- `subscribe_lock_codes` keeps `slots` as the PIN view and adds `credentials.password`: one entry per managed user holding a password on this lock.

**Cards**
- **Slot card:** layout A. Tabs appear only when there's more than one type, and each tab's dot shows that type's sync state. Only the value field changes per tab. The edit input takes `inputmode` per type (`numeric` for PIN, `text` for password), and a length hint under it comes from the lock ranges.
- **Add-user card:** the same tabs on its credential input, and the generator works per type.
- **Lock card:** type tabs. The PIN tab is today's card, and the Password tab lists users.

**Testing.** I'll follow your order: property, then end-to-end, then integration, then unit.
- **Property:** the Hypothesis stateful sync property runs over `(slot, type)` addresses with both types. The invariants: each type converges independently, a lock without password never gets a password address, and release leaves no LCM credential behind on the lock.
- **End-to-end:** Virtual, which advertises every type, plus Z-Wave. The Z-Wave fixture is **a real node dump of a User Credential CC lock that advertises password**, cited by source and not hand-built. If none exists, I'll stop and ask rather than make one up.
- **Mutation checks:** the per-lock address filter, release removing the password, the "lowest index no user holds" rule, and "a clear disables only when no credential remains".

**PR order.** These all land on a branch, and the minor release ships after PR 4.
1. **Re-key the core to `CredentialAddress`, plus the Store v2 migration.** No behavior change, since every address is still PIN. That makes the existing suite a strict oracle: any test failure is a bug.
2. **Turn on password in the model and the HA layer.** `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, per-lock addresses, the credential-required rule, the validator, the text entity split, config and services, `CREDENTIAL_LABELS`. Exercised end to end on Virtual.
3. **Z-Wave provider.** Capabilities, read, allocation on write, clear, and release.
4. **Cards.** Slot card, add-user card, lock card.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- PR 1 doing nothing visible is deliberate. It's sub-project A's "re-key with no behavior change" from the 08-16 spec, and it's the cheapest point to catch a re-keying mistake: the suite and properties are an exact oracle there, and they stop being one once PR 2 changes behavior.
- Putting Virtual before Z-Wave means PR 2 tests the type plumbing with a provider that can't misbehave. When PR 3 fails, the cause is the Z-Wave index allocation, not the core.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Does part 4 look right? If it does, I'll write the spec to `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md`. It stays local and uncommitted, since `docs/` is gitignored and your specs rule says to write specs but never commit them. Then I'll ask you to review it before the implementation plan.

# Password credentials

**Date:** 2026-10-22. **Status:** design approved in conversation; spec awaiting review.
**Base:** `origin/main` at `ce1e1088` (clean-room core merged in #1702).
**Builds on:** `2026-08-16-user-centric-credential-model-design.md` (sub-project C, never specced until now) and the 2026-09-16 multi-credential decisions (memory `project_multi_credential_types_plan`).

## Goal

A user can hold a password as well as, or instead of, a PIN. Lock Code Manager writes it to every lock in the entry that takes passwords and keeps it in sync there, the way it does PINs today.

## Scope

In:

- Password as a second managed credential type, end to end: sync core, storage, Z-Wave and Virtual providers, entities, config, services, websocket, slot card, add-user card and lock card.
- Making the core type-generic, so that RFID and NFC can later be added as data, not as structure.

Out:

- RFID, NFC and biometrics.
- A pattern on the PIN entity (see "Text entities").
- Showing or editing unmanaged passwords on the lock card.
- User Code CC locks whose keypad accepts non-digit characters. The driver uses the Password type for these (`node-zwave-js AccessControl.ts:1598`), and they may be invisible to Lock Code Manager today. Follow-up issue.

## Decisions

| # | Decision |
|---|---|
| 1 | Passwords are printable ASCII, 0x20–0x7E, spaces included. One character is one byte, so a lock's length limits mean what the user sees. On the wire, Z-Wave's credential length is a byte count (`UserCredentialCC.ts:2716`), and the driver decodes passwords as UTF-8 (`:82`). |
| 2 | The sync core is keyed by `CredentialAddress(slot, type)`. There is still one worker per lock. |
| 3 | Release stays per slot: one release removes every type Lock Code Manager wrote for the slot. |
| 4 | A slot needs at least one credential of any type. Clearing a credential disables the slot only when no other credential remains. A stored value counts even if no current lock takes its type. |
| 5 | On Z-Wave, the password index is allocated by the provider: it finds the tagged user's password wherever it is, or else takes the lowest password index no user holds. PIN keeps following the slot. |
| 6 | Credential text entities set no `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. One validator and the coordinator's per-lock length check are the only gates, and their errors never contain the value. |
| 7 | Passwords are not whitespace-stripped. PINs keep `vol.Strip`. |
| 8 | Slot card: tabs per type over one value field, each tab's dot showing that type's sync state. Tabs appear only when the entry offers more than one type. |
| 9 | Lock card: tabs per type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab lists managed users' passwords on that lock. |
| 10 | Carried from 2026-09-16: an entry's available types are the union across its locks. A type no longer offered keeps its stored value, and its entity is removed. Per-type in-sync sensors are disabled by default. Duplicates are refused within a type and allowed across types. The generator covers passwords. |

## Sync core

`CredentialAddress(user_ref, credential_type)` already exists (`model/credentials.py`). It becomes the key everywhere in `sync/`:

- `LockWorker.slots: dict[CredentialAddress, Slot]`. `want`, `forget`, `resume`, `status`, `syncing` and `push` take an address.
- `LockPort.read(addresses) -> Mapping[CredentialAddress, Reading]` and `LockPort.write(address, value) -> bool | None`.
- `sync/slot.py` stays a single-value state machine. `Holds.pin` becomes `Holds.value`, `Want` stays `str | None`, and `Holds.__repr__` keeps masking.
- `sync/registry.py` and `ha/adapter.py` re-key to match. The adapter turns an address into the provider call for that type.
- Release is per slot. When a slot leaves the entry, the worker sends one release for the slot. The provider removes every credential Lock Code Manager wrote to that slot's user, then the user only if it holds nothing else.

**Managed addresses are per lock:** `{CredentialAddress(slot, t) for t in user_types ∩ lock.capabilities.credential_types ∩ MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES}`. A lock that doesn't take password never gets a password address, so the aggregate `in_sync` on that lock ignores the type. This fixes the global `managed_addresses()` gap found in the #1572 review. Recompute when a lock is added or removed and when capabilities refresh.

`MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` becomes `{PIN, PASSWORD}`.

## Storage

`ha/lock_store.py`, `STORE_VERSION` 1 → 2.

- v1 slot record: `{"wrote": <fingerprint|cleared>, …release fields}`.
- v2 slot record: `{"wrote": {"pin": <fingerprint|cleared>, "password": <fingerprint|cleared>}, …release fields}`.
- Migration: move v1 `wrote` under `"pin"`. Release fields stay at slot level.
- The fingerprint covers the type: `fingerprint(type, value, salt)`. Credential values are never persisted.

The Store migration is the only one-way step. Downgrading leaves a v2 Store the old version can't read, and HA's Store versioning is there to refuse that.

## Configuration and the credential-required rule

- The user subentry gets an optional `password` (absent means none), and setup YAML gets `password:` per user. No config-entry migration is needed.
- The rule changes in four places:
  - `ha/slot_coordinator.py:294`: clearing any credential disables an enabled slot only if no other credential remains.
  - `ha/slot_coordinator.py:355`: enabling is refused only when the user has no credential of any type. `PinRequiredError` becomes `CredentialRequiredError`.
  - `config_flow.py:84-93, 422`: `_slot_enabled_without_pin` becomes `_slot_enabled_without_credential`, which checks every managed type's field.
  - Repair `pin_required` becomes `credential_required`. Update `switch.py:62`, `ha/services.py:451`, `repairs.py:179` and `__init__.py:1220`. At startup, delete any leftover `pin_required_*` issue.

## Providers

**Z-Wave (`providers/zwave_js.py`)**

- **Capabilities:** also report `PASSWORD` from the same `supported_credential_types` read: slot count, min/max length and `supports_learn`. A lock without password is unchanged.
- **Read `(slot, password)`:** find the user tagged `lcm:<slot>:` and return its password credential, wherever it sits, as `Holds`, `MASKED` or `EMPTY`.
- **Write:** overwrite the tagged user's password credential in place. If it has none, use the lowest password index **no user on the lock holds**, taken from the user list read just before the write, so vendor-app credentials are never overwritten. Create the user on the first write of either type, as PIN does now.
- **Clear:** delete that password credential only. The user stays.
- **Release:** delete every credential Lock Code Manager wrote to the user (PIN and password), then the user only if it holds nothing else.
- **No free index:** raise `LockOperationUnsupported`, naming the lock and its password slot count. The address holds as `CANT_SET`.

**Virtual:** already advertises every type. Its password is keyed by slot.

**Base (`providers/_base.py`):** `_assert_slot_within_capacity` stays PIN-only, because password doesn't follow the slot.

**Everyone else** (Matter, ZHA, Z2M, Schlage, Akuvox, zwave-js-ui MQTT): no change. None of them advertises password.

## Entities and validation

**Text entities (`text.py`)**

- Split `LockCodeManagerText` into `LockCodeManagerNameText` and `LockCodeManagerCredentialText(credential_type)`, with subclasses `PinText` and `PasswordText`. All credential entities use `TextMode.PASSWORD`.
- `async_set_value` calls `coordinator.async_request_credential_update(type, value)`.
- No `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. HA's own errors embed the cleartext value (`homeassistant/components/text/__init__.py:73-86`), and it re-checks them when rendering state (`:162-178`).
- Credential entities exist for the entry's available types. They're added and removed as that union changes.

**Validator:** `model/credentials.py: validate_credential_value(type, value)` checks the character set: digits for PIN, 0x20–0x7E for password. It's called from the coordinator, the config flow, `add_user`, `set_credential` and the setup YAML schema. Error text names the rule and never the value. For example: "Password may only contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces".

**Length:** `_validate_credential_length(value, type)` (`slot_coordinator.py:303`) is called for password against password-capable locks only. Its message already names each lock and its range.

**Labels:** add `"password": "Password"` to `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` (`const.py:210`) and `ts/const.ts`, which a contract test checks. That gives:
- the `password_in_sync` sensor, disabled by default (`binary_sensor.py:163`);
- password in `SENSITIVE_ENTITY_KEYS`, so diagnostics redact it;
- password in the event entity's types (`event.py:122`).

**Duplicates:** refuse a password another user in the entry already holds.

**Masking:** `mask_pin` becomes `mask_credential`, used in every log line that carries a value.

**Generator:** `generate_pin` becomes `generate_credential(type, length)`. For password it uses the printable ASCII set, at a length inside every password-capable lock's range in the entry.

## Services and websocket

- `add_user` gets `password`. `set_credential` and `clear_credential` accept `password` once it's in `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` (`ha/services.py:186`).
- `subscribe_code_slot` gets `available_types` and `credentials: {<type>: {value | length, in_sync, state}}`.
- `subscribe_lock_codes` keeps `slots` as the PIN view and adds `credentials.password`: one entry per managed user holding a password on this lock (slot, name, entry, value or length, in_sync).
- These payloads are internal. The card ships with the integration.
- Before release, check blueprints and `services.yaml` for PIN-only assumptions.

## Cards

- **Slot card (`ts/slot-card.ts`):**
  - The type tabs sit between the name and the value row. Each tab's dot shows that type's sync state: in sync, or pending or held.
  - Only the value field changes per tab. The name, enable switch, conditions and lock list stay the same.
  - The edit input sets `inputmode` per type (today it's hard-coded `numeric` at `:607`) and shows a length hint from the lock ranges.
  - With one available type, the card renders exactly as it does today.
- **Add-user card (`ts/add-user-card.ts`):** the same tabs on the credential input, with a per-type generator.
- **Lock card (`ts/lock-codes-card.ts`):** the type tabs appear when the lock takes more than one managed type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab has one chip per managed user, with no empty-position ranges and no unmanaged editing.

## Testing

Order: property, then end-to-end, then integration, then unit.

- **Property:** the Hypothesis stateful sync property runs over `(slot, type)` addresses with both types. Invariants:
  - each type converges independently;
  - a lock without password never gets a password address;
  - after release, no Lock Code Manager credential remains on the lock.
- **End-to-end:** Virtual for all types. Z-Wave uses a **sourced** node dump of a User Credential CC lock that advertises password, cited by source. If none exists, stop and ask rather than make one up.
- **Leak test:** submit an invalid value carrying a unique marker. Assert the marker appears in neither the raised error nor `caplog`.
- **Mutation checks:** the per-lock address filter, release removing the password, the "lowest index no user holds" rule, and "a clear disables only when no credential remains".

## PR order

Each PR is reviewed on its own. The minor release ships after PR 4.

1. **Core re-key to `CredentialAddress`, plus Store v2.** No behavior change, since every address is PIN, so the existing suite and properties are a strict oracle.
2. **Password in the model and HA layer:** `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, per-lock addresses, the credential-required rule, the validator, the text entity split, config and services, `CREDENTIAL_LABELS`. Exercised on Virtual.
3. **Z-Wave provider:** capabilities, read, allocation on write, clear, release.
4. **Cards:** slot card, add-user card, lock card.

## Open items

- The sourced Z-Wave User Credential CC dump with password capability (blocks PR 3 tests).
- The follow-up issue for User Code CC alphanumeric locks.

| 4 | A slot needs at least one credential of any type. Clearing a credential disables the slot only when no other credential remains. A stored value counts even if no current lock takes its type. |

| 6 | Credential text entities set no `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. One validator and the coordinator's per-lock length check are the only gates, and their errors never contain the value. |
| 7 | Passwords are not whitespace-stripped. PINs keep `vol.Strip`. |

Per-type in-sync sensors are disabled by default. Duplicates are refused within a type and allowed across types. The generator covers passwords. |

- `LockWorker.slots: dict[CredentialAddress, Slot]`. `want`, `forget`, `resume`, `status`, `syncing` and `push` take an address.

- The user subentry gets an optional `password` (absent means none), and setup YAML gets `password:` per user. No config-entry migration is needed.

- **Read `(slot, password)`:** find the user tagged `lcm:<slot>:` and return its password credential, wherever it sits, as `Holds`, `MASKED` or `EMPTY`.
- **Write:** overwrite the tagged user's password credential in place. - **Clear:** delete that password credential only. The user stays.

**Validator:** `model/credentials.py: validate_credential_value(type, value)` checks the character set: digits for PIN, 0x20–0x7E for password. It's called from the coordinator, the config flow, `add_user`, `set_credential` and the setup YAML schema. Error text names the rule and never the value. **Length:** `_validate_credential_length(value, type)` (`slot_coordinator.py:303`) is called for password against password-capable locks only. Its message already names each lock and its range.

- password in the event entity's types (`event.py:122`).

**Masking:** `mask_pin` becomes `mask_credential`, used in every log line that carries a value.

**Generator:** `generate_pin` becomes `generate_credential(type, length)`. For password it uses the printable ASCII set, at a length inside every password-capable lock's range in the entry.

- `add_user` gets `password`. `set_credential` and `clear_credential` accept `password` once it's in `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` (`ha/services.py:186`).
- `subscribe_code_slot` gets `available_types` and `credentials: {<type>: {value | length, in_sync, state}}`.
- `subscribe_lock_codes` keeps `slots` as the PIN view and adds `credentials.password`: one entry per managed user holding a password on this lock (slot, name, entry, value or length, in_sync).
- These payloads are internal. The card ships with the integration.
- Before release, check blueprints and `services.yaml` for PIN-only assumptions.

- **Slot card (`ts/slot-card.ts`):**
  - The type tabs sit between the name and the value row. Each tab's dot shows that type's sync state: in sync, or pending or held.
  - Only the value field changes per tab. The name, enable switch, conditions and lock list stay the same.
  - The edit input sets `inputmode` per type (today it's hard-coded `numeric` at `:607`) and shows a length hint from the lock ranges.
  - With one available type, the card renders exactly as it does today.
- **Add-user card (`ts/add-user-card.ts`):** the same tabs on the credential input, with a per-type generator.
- **Lock card (`ts/lock-codes-card.ts`):** the type tabs appear when the lock takes more than one managed type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab has one chip per managed user, with no empty-position ranges and no unmanaged editing.

Order: property, then end-to-end, then integration, then unit.

- **Property:** the Hypothesis stateful sync property runs over `(slot, type)` addresses with both types. Invariants:

  - a lock without password never gets a password address;
  - after release, no Lock Code Manager credential remains on the lock.

- **Leak test:** submit an invalid value carrying a unique marker. Assert the marker appears in neither the raised error nor `caplog`.
- **Mutation checks:** the per-lock address filter, release removing the password, the "lowest index no user holds" rule, and "a clear disables only when no credential remains".

Each PR is reviewed on its own. The minor release ships after PR 4.

1. **Core re-key to `CredentialAddress`, plus Store v2.** No behavior change, since every address is PIN, so the existing suite and properties are a strict oracle.
2. **Password in the model and HA layer:** `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, per-lock addresses, the credential-required rule, the validator, the text entity split, config and services, `CREDENTIAL_LABELS`. Exercised on Virtual.
3. **Z-Wave provider:** capabilities, read, allocation on write, clear, release.
4. **Cards:** slot card, add-user card, lock card.

## Open items

- The sourced Z-Wave User Credential CC dump with password capability (blocks PR 3 tests).
- The follow-up issue for User Code CC alphanumeric locks.

I've written the spec to `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md`. It's not committed: `docs/` is gitignored and your rule is to keep specs local.

While reviewing it I fixed one mistake that came from part 1. I'd written that a lock manages password only for users who **have** a password. It actually has to manage it for **every** user wherever the lock takes passwords, with "wanted: nothing" for users who have none. Otherwise a password that gets removed is never cleared from the lock, which is the #1453 problem (a deleted user's code still opens the door) for a second type. PIN already works this way, because an empty PIN is actively kept cleared today.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- In this core, "nothing wanted" is a real target, not the absence of one. A slot whose `want` is `None` is still synced, toward empty. That's why the address set follows what the lock can hold, not what the user has.
- The spec's "Decisions" table is the part to protect. It records several choices with the evidence behind them, like dropping the pattern because HA's errors include the value. Those are the ones most likely to get re-argued halfway through implementation.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

I also saved the decisions to memory (`project_password_credential_design`), so a later session picks them up without re-deciding them.

Please review the spec and tell me what to change. Once you approve it, I'll write the implementation plan. One thing blocks the tests for PR 3 (the Z-Wave provider): they need a real node dump from a User Credential CC lock that advertises password. If you have one, or know where one is, that would help.

content.thinking: This is just a summary, so I'll keep the response short without needing a deeper insight block.

content.text:
**Password support: the short version**

- **What:** a user can have a PIN, a password, or both. LCM writes the password to every lock in the entry that accepts passwords and keeps it in sync, the same way it does PINs.
- **Which locks:** Z-Wave User Credential CC locks and Virtual. Nothing changes for Matter, ZHA, Z2M, Schlage or Akuvox.
- **Allowed characters:** printable ASCII, spaces included, never trimmed. Validation happens only in LCM's own code. The text entities set no pattern or min/max length, because HA's errors would show the password in plain text.
- **Core change:** the sync engine tracks each user's credentials by (slot, type) instead of by slot alone. Each lock still has a single worker. Locks that don't support passwords never get one.
- **Storage:** the record of what was written gains a per-type field, with a one-way upgrade of the Store file.
- **Enable rule:** a user needs at least one credential of any type. Clearing one only disables the user if nothing else is left.
- **Z-Wave password position:** Z-Wave picks the password's position on the lock itself, using a position no other user has, so it never overwrites codes added outside LCM. PINs still sit at the slot number.
- **Removing a user:** deletes both the PIN and the password from the lock.
- **Slot card:** PIN and Password tabs over one input box. A dot on each tab shows whether that credential is in sync. With only one type available, the card looks the same as today.
- **Lock card:** the same tabs. The PIN tab is today's view, and the Password tab lists users.
- **Order of work:**
  1. Restructure the sync core with no visible change.
  2. Turn on passwords, tested on Virtual.
  3. Add Z-Wave support.
  4. Update the cards.

  Releases as a minor version.
- **Blocker:** the Z-Wave tests need a real dump from a User Credential CC lock that supports passwords.

The full spec is in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md`.

aiTitle: Credential types in docs and specs

content.thinking: Confirmed there's no password credential type in Matter - the available types are Programming PIN, PIN, RFID, Fingerprint, FingerVein, Face, and Aliro keys, so there's nothing to write for a password field.

content.text:
It's not something we decided to leave out. **Matter has no password credential type**, so there is nothing for LCM to write. The DoorLock cluster's `CredentialTypeEnum` in the Matter SDK (`chip/clusters/cluster_defs/DoorLock.py:159-168`) lists only:

| Value | Type |
|---|---|
| 0x00 | ProgrammingPIN (the admin code) |
| 0x01 | PIN |
| 0x02 | RFID |
| 0x03 | Fingerprint |
| 0x04 | FingerVein |
| 0x05 | Face |
| 0x06–0x08 | Aliro keys (phone/wallet credentials) |

Z-Wave's User Credential CC has a separate Password type (`UserCredentialType.Password = 0x02`). Matter doesn't, so Z-Wave and Virtual are the only providers where password exists.

**RFID is the second type Matter does have**, and LCM's Matter provider already knows about it: `matter.py:112-117` maps `kRfid` when reading, and `matter.py:813-818` builds an RFID capability. The design keys everything by (slot, type) and works out per lock which types it can hold, so adding RFID later is mostly a matter of:

- including RFID in `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`;
- Matter writing RFID credentials (its index is already allocated by the lock);
- a validator rule for RFID values (hex);
- an "RFID" label, which brings the entity, the in-sync sensor and the card tab with it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Credential *types* differ between protocols even where the *concept* overlaps. A Matter lock with a full keyboard still stores what you type as a PIN credential. So a password made of letters could only reach a Matter lock as a "PIN", and LCM won't change a value's type to fit a lock.
- This is why the per-lock address rule matters. An entry with one Z-Wave lock and one Matter lock offers both tabs, but a password is only written to the Z-Wave lock. That lock's `in_sync` covers the password; the Matter lock's covers only the PIN.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Should I add a line to the spec's scope section recording that Matter has no password type (with the SDK citation), so nobody reopens it as a gap?

## T3 Code orchestration

The `t3-code` MCP server provides app-owned orchestration. Treat these concepts distinctly:

- A delegated task/subagent is child work owned by the current thread. Use `orchestrator_capabilities` to discover the current provider/model IDs from the same live catalog as the composer, including configured custom models. Do not treat a native tool's model list as the full list of available subagent models. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use `delegate_task` with that provider instance and model when native tools cannot, including for same-provider work. Also use `delegate_task` for cross-provider or explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For a child task that needs a separate checkout, use `delegate_task` with `isolation:"worktree"` across any provider or model. It starts from the parent local commit and runs project setup; uncommitted edits are not copied. Retain each returned `taskId`, and use `task_status` or `task_cancel` to manage it. The returned `childThreadId` is backing storage for the subagent, not the target for starting another delegated review round.
- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` create ordinary top-level T3 conversations. Use them only when the user explicitly asks for separate/new/top-level threads or conversations. Never use them merely because the user said "subagent" or requested parallel delegated work.
- For every T3 delegated review round, call `delegate_task` again. Include the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in each new task prompt. Track each round by its own `taskId`. Use a distinct `clientRequestId` per round, stable across retries of that round. Do not use `t3_thread_send` on `childThreadId` to continue a delegated review.

- `schedule_task` creates persistent recurring work in the app scheduler. Pass `schedule` as a structured object, never as JSON text: `{"type":"interval","everyMs":3600000}` for an interval, or `{"type":"fixed_time","timeOfDay":"09:00","weekdays":[1,2,3,4,5]}` for a wall-clock schedule, or `{"type":"webhook"}` to run on each request to the returned `webhookUrl` (the run sees the request only through `{{body.path}}`-style placeholders in the prompt). By default runs return to the current thread, which suits orchestrating: each trigger arrives here and you delegate or dedupe; set `bindToCurrentThread=false` only when the user wants a fresh thread for every run. After scheduling a timer, report the returned cadence and next run time; for a webhook, report its `webhookUrl`, or say T3 Connect remote access is needed if it is missing.
- When you need a secret from the user (a token, API key, or webhook signing secret), call `request_secret` so they enter it privately, then pass the returned `secretRef` to the tool that needs it, e.g. `signature.secretRef` on a webhook task for a sender that signs requests such as GitHub. A `secretRef` works once. Never ask for a secret in chat, never invent one, and never repeat one.
- To mention another thread to the user, link it as `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with its exact `threadId`, not URL-encoded. T3 Code opens the thread in the app and shows its current title.

### Choose the workspace before starting a new thread

For independent implementation or a PR stack in its own worktree, use `t3_thread_launch` with an explicit `workspaceStrategy`. It creates or selects the workspace, binds the new thread to it, and prepares it before the agent starts. Put the task in `message`, not `prompt`:

- New worktree: `{"title":"UI cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"worktree","baseRef":"feature/base","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup","startFromOrigin":false},"message":"Implement the cleanup and open a PR against feature/base."}`
- Existing worktree: `{"title":"Continue cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"existing_worktree","worktreePath":"/absolute/path/to/worktree","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup"},"message":"Continue the cleanup."}`
- Project's main checkout: `workspaceStrategy:{"type":"root"}`. Omitting workspaceStrategy also selects root; it does not inherit the caller's worktree.

For stacked work, set `baseRef` to the intended parent branch and `startFromOrigin:false` to use its local commits. Use `startFromOrigin:true` when you intend to fetch the base branch's remote and start from it. Uncommitted edits are not copied. Use `t3_worktree_list` to discover existing checkout paths. Project, model selection, and modes inherit unless supplied; a launched thread may not run with broader modes than yours.

`t3_thread_launch` is the single-thread launch tool. Use `create_threads` only for a batch of threads intentionally sharing the caller's checkout: it always inherits the caller's project, branch, and worktree and has no workspace override. Asking an agent to run `git worktree add` or `cd` in its prompt does not update T3's thread binding. Select the workspace in the launch call instead. `t3_worktree_handoff` moves the calling thread, not another thread, and cannot move a thread already attached to a worktree.

`t3_thread_launch` has no idempotency key. Retain its returned threadId and inspect it with `t3_thread_read` / `t3_thread_wait`; preparation can still be running after acceptance. If a launch fails or its response is lost, inspect `t3_thread_list` before retrying, since a thread may already exist.

Tool names may include a harness-normalized MCP prefix, such as `mcp__t3_code__delegate_task`; the semantics are the same. Some harnesses attach optional MCP servers lazily: if an initial tool-catalog scan does not show T3 tools, do not conclude that cross-provider delegation is unavailable. Make one bounded direct attempt using the known T3 tool name on the next tool step. In Codex code mode, for example, call `tools.mcp__t3_code__orchestrator_capabilities({})` before reporting that the capability is absent. Keep polling/wait loops bounded, do not duplicate active work, and use stable `clientRequestId` values when retrying tools that accept them.

ACP fallback: some ACP agents accept the injected MCP server but fail to expose its tools. When the T3 tools are absent and `T3_ACP_MCP_NODE` is present, call the same tools through the terminal: `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$T3_ACP_MCP_NODE" ${T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT:+"$T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT"} acp-mcp-call orchestrator_capabilities '{}'` (`T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT` is unset when T3 runs as a standalone executable). Delegate with `acp-mcp-call delegate_task '{"task":"...","target":{"providerInstanceId":"...","model":"..."},"mode":"async","clientRequestId":"..."}'`. This is the supported T3 transport fallback, not an ordinary shell-based substitute for delegation.

### Showing visuals

When a chart, table, diagram, image collage, or mockup would say more than prose, build a self-contained HTML page, check it with `html_preview`, then publish it with `html_render` before your final reply. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

- When model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty `inheritedOptions` from `orchestrator_capabilities`, use `delegate_task` even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Read the selected model's descriptors from `orchestrator_capabilities` and put settings in `target.options`, not only in the prompt. Claude commonly uses {"effort":"max","fastMode":true}; Codex uses {"reasoningEffort":"max","serviceTier":"priority"}. Do not translate max to high or ignore unsupported settings: report a capability mismatch. Options inherit only for the same provider instance and model; explicit entries override individual values, and [] or {} clears them. Check the returned providerInstanceId, model, and options against the requested selection.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_preview
tools.description: Render an HTML page in T3's headless browser and get back a PNG screenshot, contentHeight (the height the page needs at this width), and its console output: log, info, warning, error, and uncaught exceptions, with stack traces pointing into page.html. console.log is a fine way to report your own checks. Use it to check and iterate on a page before html_render. The first preview on a machine can report that T3 is still installing its preview browser; call again a minute later. Write one self-contained document with inline <style> and <script>. Local images written as absolute file paths (src="/abs/shot.png", CSS url(/abs/bg.webp), or a JS string) are inlined automatically; remote http(s) URLs, such as a CDN chart library, load as-is. The page gets the theme variables and layout described in html_render.

anyOf.description: Viewport width in CSS pixels, 240-1600. Defaults to 728, the reply column; use about 390 to check phones.
Theme to preview. Defaults to dark.
